newsitem.title: USA: Trial brought McVeigh's views to wider audience.
newsitem.headline: Trial brought McVeigh's views to wider audience.

text.p: Despite being sentenced to death on Friday for blowing up an Oklahoma City federal building, Timothy McVeigh may have scored one hollow victory in an otherwise lop-sided trial, legal analysts say.
McVeigh succeeded in spreading his view that the 1993 siege at Waco, Texas, was an act of government-sanctioned war against innocent civilians.

"(McVeigh) was able to use his trial...to air those same beliefs that he was attempting to misguidedly advance by blowing up the federal building. So there's a cruel irony there that he actually got his way," Denver trial attorney Scott Robinson, who closely followed the trial, said.

Prosecutors said McVeigh was a right-wing fanatic who blew up the Alfred P. Murrah building, killing 168 people, to avenge the deaths of about 80 Branch Davidian cult members in a showdown with federal agents at Waco two years earlier.
The defence tried to persuade the jury to spare McVeigh's life by explaining why the ex-soldier believed the government murdered the Branch Davidians and their leader David Koresh.

For more than a day, the defence played videos for the jurors and told them about articles in "Soldier of Fortune" magazine and elsewhere that were critical of the government's actions at Waco. They were the same videos and articles that McVeigh was influenced by.

The jury watched an hour-long video, "Day 51, The True Story of Waco," featuring scenes of the fire that destroyed the cult compound and ended the 51-day siege. Jurors were told of the belief in right-wing circles that the government was to blame for the violence.

Several jurors seemed bored by the Waco testimony and some legal analysts thought the defence strategy could backfire if the jury believed it was trying to justify the bombing. On Friday, the jury called for McVeigh to be sentenced to death.
But McVeigh had the satisfaction of seeing his views on Waco reach a wider audience, carried beyond the courtroom by media reports of the trial.

Robinson said he believed McVeigh himself demanded that the Waco evidence be part of the defence case. "I think he was the architect. I think he was pulling those strings. It is his life after all. If he wants to be a martyr, what better way?"
McVeigh, 29, did not testify during his trial.

The defence called relatives, neighbours and friends of McVeigh who painted a picture of a cheerful, caring young man who showed an early interest in guns. Former Army colleagues said he was a model soldier during his three-and-a-half year stint in the service, including Gulf War duty.

But legal analysts said the defence had an uphill struggle convincing the jury to opt for life imprisonment in the face of the heart-wrenching testimony presented by the prosecution during its campaign for the death penalty.

For more than two days, survivors and relatives of bombing victims gave searing testimony about the horror of the explosion, the loss of loved ones and the physical and emotional scars the attack left behind.

Christopher Mueller, a law professor at the University of Colorado, said the defence succeeded in humanising McVeigh "and conveying to the jury the sense that this is a man who led a life that has positive values..."

The Waco testimony was meant to suggest that McVeigh was by no means alone in being seriously concerned about the siege, Mueller said. "It brings home an explanation for this crime. It isn't an excuse...but it explains why he did it," he said.

But Robert Precht, director of the Office of Public Service at the Univeristy of Michigan law school, said he believed the defence "diluted the impact of the evidence that tended to humanise him (McVeigh) by putting on this evidence about Waco."

"To me...it veered dangerously into suggesting that he had a political motivation to do what he did and that seems to be inconsistent with a strategy of humanising," said Precht, who represented one of the defendants in the World Trade Centre bombing case.
